title: The journal cap that didn't cap
role: You maintain a Linux image (built with Yocto, systemd 243) that runs on many small devices. The persistent journal is capped with SystemMaxUse=128M so it can't fill the disk.

source.label: systemd/systemd #14583: Journal doesn't respect SystemMaxUse option (GitHub issue)

brief: A test device reports low disk space. `/var/log/journal` is at 169M, more than its 128M cap, and still growing. journald itself claims it is well under the limit.

steps.situation: journald and du disagree by a factor of ten.
steps.evidence:
$ grep -E 'Storage|MaxUse' /etc/systemd/journald.conf
Storage=persistent
SystemMaxUse=128M
RuntimeMaxUse=64M
$ journalctl -b -u systemd-journald | grep 'System Journal'
... System Journal (/var/log/journal/4f1c...) is 16.0M, max 128.0M, 112.0M free.
$ sudo du -sh /var/log/journal
169M	/var/log/journal

choices.text: Look one level down: du per subdirectory, and count them
choices.why: journald's 16M is for one directory. If du says 169M, something else is in `/var/log/journal`.
journald already thinks it uses 16M. A lower cap trims that one directory and leaves the rest.
The space comes back, the logs you'd need to understand the problem don't, and it will fill again.

steps.situation: There are twelve subdirectories, each 8 to 25M, each named with 32 hex characters.
steps.evidence:
$ sudo du -sh /var/log/journal/* | sort -h | tail -3
19M	/var/log/journal/a07e...
22M	/var/log/journal/5bd2...
25M	/var/log/journal/e93f...
$ ls /var/log/journal | wc -l
12
$ cat /etc/machine-id
4f1c...

choices.why: journald names its directory after the machine ID. Twelve directories means the ID has changed eleven times, and journald only manages the current one.

choices.text: Delete the biggest directories by size
choices.why: You might delete the active one and keep the orphans, and you still don't know why there are twelve.

choices.text: It's a journald bug: report it and wait for a fix
choices.why: The maintainer closed exactly this report as not-a-bug: the setup was the problem.

steps.situation: The image gives the device a fresh machine ID on every boot, but `/var` survives reboots. What do you change?

choices.text: Keep /etc/machine-id stable (create it once, keep it), or, if it must change each boot, wipe /var each boot too
choices.why: The maintainer's answer: a random ID per boot is supported only on fully stateless systems where `/var` is flushed as well.

choices.text: Add a cron job that deletes old journal directories
choices.why: It treats the symptom. Anything else keyed on the machine ID keeps changing every boot.
The disk is safe and you are blind on every device in the field.

steps.situation: The image now keeps its machine ID. Eleven orphaned directories remain on each device.

choices.text: Delete every directory whose name isn't the current machine ID, then check du against the cap
choices.why: journald never touches them, so nobody else will. Leave the current one to journald's own cap and vacuum.

choices.text: Leave them: the cap works now
choices.why: The cap covers only the current directory. The old 150M stays used forever.

choices.text: Run journalctl --vacuum-size=100M and assume it covers all
choices.why: Check with du afterwards. Don't assume a tool cleans up directories its daemon has stopped managing.

debrief.what_happened: In January 2020 a user of systemd 243 on a Yocto system reported that the persistent journal ignored `SystemMaxUse=128M`. journald reported its system journal as 16.0M of 128.0M, but `du` showed 169M in `/var/log/journal`, spread over 12 directories named after machine IDs. Lennart Poettering pointed at the likely cause, an unstable `/etc/machine-id`: journald names its directory after it, and when the ID changes, journald starts a new directory and never cleans up the old ones. Random machine IDs are supported on stateless systems only if `/var` is also flushed on every boot; a changing ID with a persistent `/var` is not a supported mode. The issue was labelled not-a-bug and closed the same day without a code change. The fix is operational: keep the machine ID stable (or make `/var` stateless too) and remove the orphaned directories.
lessons: SystemMaxUse limits journald's current directory, not everything under /var/log/journal.
Many journal directories = a machine ID that keeps changing.
Images and VM templates must handle /etc/machine-id on purpose.
When the tool and du disagree, look one directory level deeper.
